records.quote: Death, barring accidents, was an adventure for volunteers.
records.paraphrase: Because aging is cured, death now only comes to those who volunteer for it.

records.quote:
Now
centuries of peace and plenty stretch before us as far as the
imagination cares to travel.
records.paraphrase: Hitz frames population control as producing lasting peace and abundance.

records.quote:
He corrected
himself, gave the municipal gas chambers their official title, a title
no one ever used in conversation. "I should have said, 'Ethical Suicide
Studios,'"
records.paraphrase: Euphemistic official term 'Ethical Suicide Studios' is used for the termination facilities.

records.quote:
In the year 2000," said Dr. Hitz, "before scientists stepped in and
laid down the law, there wasn't even enough drinking water to go around,
and nothing to eat but sea-weed
records.paraphrase: Hitz recounts a past crisis of water and food scarcity that scientists addressed.

records.quote: "I want those kids," said Wehling quietly. "I want all three of them."
records.paraphrase: Wehling emotionally resists giving up any of his children.

records.quote:
"To be or not to be" was the telephone number of the municipal gas
chambers of the Federal Bureau of Termination.
records.paraphrase: A government bureau operates voluntary termination gas chambers reachable by phone.

records.quote:
There were no prisons, no slums, no insane asylums, no cripples, no
poverty, no wars.
records.paraphrase: Society has eliminated prisons, poverty, and war.

records.quote:
The law said that no newborn child could survive unless the parents of
the child could find someone who would volunteer to die. Triplets, if
they were all to live, called for three volunteers.
records.paraphrase: Law requires a volunteer death for each newborn to be allowed to live.

records.quote:
He knew that he would never paint again. He let his paintbrush fall to
the dropcloths below.
records.paraphrase: The painter is so affected he abandons painting.

records.quote:
Wehling was fifty-six, a mere stripling in a population whose average
age was one hundred and twenty-nine.
records.paraphrase: The average lifespan is now extremely long, making 56 young.

records.quote: All diseases were conquered. So was old age.
records.paraphrase: Disease and aging have been eliminated.

records.quote:
Wehling shot Dr. Hitz dead. "There's room for one--a great big one," he
said.
records.paraphrase: Wehling kills Dr. Hitz to create room for a child.

records.quote:
The population of the United States was stabilized at forty-million
souls.
records.paraphrase: The national population is held fixed at forty million.

records.quote:
"You think this is my idea of what life really looks
like?"
records.paraphrase: The painter contrasts the idealized mural with the true nature of life.

records.quote: And then he shot himself, making room for all three of his children.
records.paraphrase: Wehling kills himself and others to allow his triplets to live.

records.quote:
Would you like to go back to the good old days, when the population of
the Earth was twenty billion--about to become forty billion, then eighty
billion, then one hundred and sixty billion?
records.paraphrase: Uncontrolled population would have grown to extreme numbers.

records.quote:
Without population
control, human beings would now be packed on this surface of this old
planet like drupelets on a blackberry!
records.paraphrase: Hitz explains overcrowding as the rationale for population control.

criteria.rationale: The conquest of disease and old age, and scientists' intervention on water/food scarcity and overpopulation, materially represent speculative biological and demographic science underpinning the storyworld.

The municipal gas chambers are an engineered institutional system central to the setting, but the story treats them more as social apparatus than as a described invention; X-rays and telephones are ordinary. Materiality as a distinct technology is uncertain.
The story is set in a speculative future where the cure for aging yields average ages of 129 and characters two centuries old, an explicit future setting.
The central premise—curing aging plus limited planetary resources—is rigorously extrapolated into a mandatory one-death-per-birth population-control regime, driving the entire plot.

Scientists are referenced as having solved past problems, but no observation, hypothesis, testing, or evidential revision materially drives the narrative's understanding or action; the science is background result, not method depicted.
The story takes place on ordinary Earth (Chicago); no other planets, dimensions, nonordinary cosmic environments, or visitors appear.

A remembered/impending global catastrophe of overpopulation—twenty billion rising toward hundreds of billions with no water and only seaweed to eat—is causally central to the story's whole social order; the individual shootings alone are personal-scale, but the demographic disaster is large-scale and central.

candidates.description: A totalizing social-scientific regime in which aging and disease have been cured, making death effectively voluntary, and the population is held fixed at forty million by a law requiring a volunteer to die for each newborn to be permitted to live, administered through the Federal Bureau of Termination and its 'Ethical Suicide Studios.'

novelty.rationale: The conquest of aging and disease, an average age of 129, voluntary-only death, and a legally fixed population of forty million constitute a totalizing departure from the empirical norm, altering the fundamental terms of birth, death, and human life in the story universe.

cognitive_validation.rationale: The world is grounded in a coherent, immanent, nonsupernatural rationale: scientists conquered aging and resource scarcity, and overpopulation (the 'drupelets on a blackberry' logic and projected 20-to-160-billion growth) motivates a systematic bureaucratic one-in/one-out population-control law with dedicated institutions. It reads as a consistent social-scientific extrapolation.

narrative_hegemony.rationale: The entire plot is generated by the regime: Wehling must find volunteers so his triplets may live, and his climactic murders and suicide, plus the painter's decision to call the Bureau, are direct consequences of the one-death-per-birth law. The novum determines the overriding narrative logic.

estrangement.rationale: The euphemistic institutional apparatus ('Ethical Suicide Studios,' the Bureau of Termination, the sanitized mural 'The Happy Garden of Life') and the utopian rhetoric of 'no prisons, no wars' set against gas chambers and enforced death create sharp reader-facing contrast, estranging the reader from the ostensibly perfect society.
